outcome: No proof, disproof or credible claim about whether there are infinitely many prime Lucas numbers has appeared, and no event since 26 January 2024 bears on the question: the only in-window items are papers on neighbouring questions, and the Prime Pages top twenty's newest proven entries date from December 2023.
problem_asks: Whether there are infinitely many Lucas primes, read as: whether infinitely many Lucas numbers Lₙ (Prime Pages notation V(n) = Lₙ) are themselves prime. This is a single question about one set, the prime values of Lₙ, equivalently the indices n for which Lₙ is prime. The statement does not itself state the index condition (Lₙ prime forces n to be 0, a prime, or a power of 2); that is background, not part of what is asked. Ambiguity: 'Lucas primes' could also be read as primes occurring anywhere in Lucas sequences in the sense of Broderius and Greene. This record takes the classical reading, because the Wikipedia bullet links to the 'Lucas primes' section of the Lucas number article. The broader reading is recorded as a neighbouring question, not as this problem.

Dated 1995-03 here because that is the earliest entry in the batch; the other entries carry their own dates in the page. These are instances of the set, not progress on its infinitude.
events.delivers: Adds eleven individual prime Lucas numbers with indices from 8467 to 56003. This is a finite set of instances of a question about infinitely many, so it moves nothing about infinitude.

events.what_happened: Dubner and Keller, 'New Fibonacci and Lucas primes', Mathematics of Computation (1999). It tested Lₙ for probable primality up to n = 50000 and gave rigorous proofs for some. The Prime Pages Top Twenty page cites this paper and says: 'Probable primality of F, L, F* and L* tested for n up to 50000, 50000, 20000, and 15000, respectively.' The paper itself was not opened; the citation and quotation are from the opened Top Twenty page, and the journal page was seen only in search results.
events.revisions: Some individual discoveries credited to DK on the Top Twenty page are dated 1995, so the first public argument for those may predate the 1999 paper.
events.delivers: Probable-prime tests of Lₙ for all n up to 50000, with a few proven primes. This is a search over finitely many indices, so it gives instances and no bearing on infinitude.

events.what_happened: A comment on OEIS A001606 (indices of prime Lucas numbers) by Serge Batalov, dated 30 May 2017: 'Powers of 2 in this sequence are 2, 4, 8, 16; for 5 <= m <= 24, L(2^m) is composite...' The rest of the comment was not visible in the fetched text. This is a finite check that the candidate indices 2^m for 5 to 24 do not give prime Lucas numbers.
events.delivers: Rules out the power-of-two indices 2^5 to 2^24 as giving prime Lucas numbers. A finite range of the candidate index class, so it does not decide infinitude.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many power-of-two indices, or any other indices, give prime Lucas numbers.
events.directly_checkable: L(2^m) for 5 <= m <= 24 can be checked by anyone with a Lucas-number computation. Not checked here.
events.direction: Finitely many candidate indices ruled out. Cuts neither way on the infinitude question.

events.what_happened: Somer and Křížek, 'On primes in Lucas sequences', Fibonacci Quarterly vol. 53 (2015). The PDF could not be read here. From a search-result summary, it gives necessary and sufficient tests for the primality of Lucas-sequence terms, and states that a Lucas number Lₘ can be prime only if m is 0, a prime, or a power of 2. That index condition also appears on the Prime Pages glossary and the Wikipedia article, both opened. The date is the year of the volume; the PDF's metadata creation date is 10 February 2015.
events.delivers: Establishes the index condition for prime Lucas numbers (necessary, not sufficient). Background to the question; does not bear on infinitude.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in vol. 53 (2015); the refereeing and the paper's content were not read here

events.direction: Restricts where prime Lucas numbers can occur. Cuts neither way on infinitude.

events.what_happened: Broderius and Greene, 'Lucas sequences containing few primes', Fibonacci Quarterly vol. 59, issue 2 (May 2021), pp. 136-144. The abstract, read on the University of Minnesota research-portal page, says that 'proving that a Lucas sequence contains infinitely many primes is a difficult problem', gives 'two families of Lucas sequences containing only finitely many primes', and conjectures that 'all other Lucas sequences without obvious obstructions contain infinitely many primes'. A search summary adds that proving infinitude is beyond current techniques for any Lucas sequence other than two specific ones; that sentence is not visible in the abstract and the PDF was not readable.
events.revisions: Only the journal issue date is established. An earlier public version may exist (the PDF file name carries '2020'); not verified.
events.delivers: For Lucas sequences in the general sense, finitely many primes in two families; a conjecture of infinitude for the rest. The abstract does not say whether the classical Lucas numbers Lₙ belong to either family, so this is not established. As far as the abstract goes, it does not settle the classical question.
events.remains: The classical question: whether infinitely many Lₙ are prime. Also the general conjecture for Lucas sequences.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in vol. 59 issue 2; refereeing not inspected

events.direction: Negative for two families of Lucas sequences (finitely many primes); positive conjecture for the rest. Whether this reaches the classical Lₙ is not established from the abstract.

events.what_happened: Ismailescu, Jeon, Kim, Kwon and Lee, 'Shifting Lucas sequences away from primes', Integers 25 (2025), article A42, published April 2025 per a search-result summary. The PDF was not readable here, so the content below is from a search summary and is unverified. It says that for every positive integer P there is a positive integer K(P) such that the shifted sequence Uₙ(P,1) + K(P) has no primes and no terms one unit from a prime, strengthening a result of Jones; and that for Q = 1 and P at least 3, all but finitely many of Uₙ − 1, Uₙ and Uₙ + 1 are composite.
events.revisions: A search summary gives 'received July 2022' and 'revised December 2024' for the journal. These are not public dates. No public version before 2025 was found, so the year 2025 is an upper bound on the first public argument, not a verified date.
events.delivers: Per the search summary: shifted Lucas sequences that avoid primes. The object is a shifted sequence Uₙ(P,Q) + K, not the Lucas numbers Lₙ and not their prime values. It is a neighbouring question.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in April 2025 per the search summary; the PDF was not read here

events.direction: Cuts toward finitely many or no primes, but for shifted sequences, a different object. No bearing on the infinitude of prime Lucas numbers.

events.what_happened: Hayder Hashim (University of Kufa), 'Generalized Lucas primes in the Fermat-Euler equation', Journal of Algebraic Systems vol. 14, issue 2 (April 2026), pp. 317-330. The abstract page, opened, asks 'whether or not this form keeps the property of generating infinitely many primes' when the unknowns are terms of Lucas sequences, and frames the work as integer solutions of p = x² + dy² with x, y, p Lucas terms. It makes no claim that the prime Lucas numbers Lₙ are infinite.
events.revisions: The page gives only the issue date. A search summary says 'received January 2024', which is not on the page and is not a public date. The first public version was not located.
events.delivers: Integer solutions of p = x² + dy² with Lucas-sequence unknowns, under conditions on a and b. It is a different question that uses the name 'generalized Lucas primes'. No claim on the infinitude of prime Lucas numbers.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in April 2026; the page lists no referee information, and refereeing was not verified

events.direction: No bearing on the classical question. It asks a different question about a different family of primes.

events.what_happened: Herbert Batte, 'On Wagstaff primes in the k-Lucas number sequence', arXiv:2602.20387 (math.NT), submitted 23 February 2026. The abstract, opened, states that the only solutions of L_n^(k) = (2^p + 1)/3 are (n, k, p) in {(5, 2, 5), (6, 4, 7)} together with (2, k, 3) for k ≥ 2, obtained by linear forms in logarithms and LLL reduction.
events.delivers: A complete finite list of solutions for k-Lucas numbers with k ≥ 2 that equal Wagstaff numbers. It is about a different family (k ≥ 2), not the classical Lₙ, and it makes no claim on the infinitude of any prime sequence.
events.direction: No bearing on the classical question. A finite Diophantine result on a different sequence family.

events.what_happened: Poo-Sung Park, 'The Fibonacci numbers are not an additive uniqueness set for multiplicative functions', arXiv:2609.08137, v1 submitted 8 September 2026. The abstract, opened, says the paper shows a multiplicative function f need not be the identity even when it takes positive integer values, answering negatively a question of Spiro (1992); the smallest example comes from F₃₁ = 557 · 2417. It says the paper 'describe[s] the AI-assisted search that led to the construction', and the comments field says '7 pages, AI-assisted'. No model is named in the abstract or comments. The PDF body was unreadable.
events.delivers: A counterexample to a Fibonacci-number uniqueness question for multiplicative functions. It concerns Fibonacci numbers, not Lucas numbers or their prime values. No bearing on the classical question.
events.directly_checkable: The abstract says a reproducible certificate checker is provided, which would check the example; not run here.
events.doubts: Unreviewed preprint. The AI-assisted role is described only in the abstract and comments, and no model is named in any text I could read. A search summary of the body names an OpenAI model and an interactive ChatGPT session, but I could not read the body, so that name is not recorded.
events.direction: Counterexample to a Fibonacci-number question, cutting against a statement about multiplicative functions, not about Lucas primes.
events.object: The smallest example is a multiplicative function built from the factorisation F₃₁ = 557 · 2417 with a fourth-power criterion for further examples; the abstract states that the construction is explicit and checkable by a certificate checker.

summary: Thirty-seven searches (listed verbatim below) and opened sources found no event since 26 January 2024 that bears on whether there are infinitely many prime Lucas numbers, and no proof, disproof or credible claim about it. The Wikipedia bullet 'Are there infinitely many Lucas primes?' is in the unsolved list and links to the 'Lucas primes' section of the Lucas number article; that article and the Prime Pages glossary both record it as open and conjectured infinite. The evidence that nothing happened in the window is: (1) the Prime Pages Top Twenty for prime Lucas numbers, opened, whose newest entries are from November and December 2023, and which states that larger ones will be added when found (the page is undated, so its currency is not established); (2) the OEIS index list A001606 and its dated comments, opened, whose latest dated line is from 2017, with no dated 2024 to 2026 additions, although the index list itself has no per-term dates; (3) the OEIS sequence A005479, opened, with no comment on infinitude; (4) about thirty searches for AI involvement, none of which tied a Lucas-prime result to an AI system. The in-window items are all neighbouring questions, each recorded as discounted: a 2025 Integers paper on prime-free shifted Lucas sequences (its PDF was not readable; its content is from a search summary); a 2026 arXiv paper on Wagstaff primes in k-Lucas sequences for k ≥ 2 (abstract opened); a 2026 Journal of Algebraic Systems paper on 'generalized Lucas primes' in the Fermat-Euler equation (abstract page opened); and a September 2026 arXiv paper on Fibonacci numbers and multiplicative functions whose abstract says it used an 'AI-assisted search' without naming a model. Close calls. (a) Whether a shifted-sequence or generalized-prime result counts as 'Lucas primes' depends on the reading of the statement; I took the classical reading, so both are recorded as different questions. (b) Whether probable-prime additions to the index list would move anything: none dated inside the window were found, and even if one were, under the scope rule it is one more instance of a question about infinitely many. (c) The 2026 cofactor record V(277273)/11090921 (May 2026) is a proper divisor of a Lucas number, not a prime, so it is excluded. The AI search found no AI system credited with a Lucas-prime result. The AI-related prime claims that surfaced (Axiom's 246 prime-gap bound and an OpenAI 186 preprint, both on prime gaps, and several Erdős problems) are about other problems and were seen only in search summaries, so they are not recorded as events.
competing_reading: Read 'Lucas primes' as primes occurring anywhere in Lucas sequences (the Broderius and Greene sense). On that reading the 2021 two-family dichotomy and the 2025 shifted-sequence result are real movement on a named quantity, since they settle finitely many families and show infinitude is out of current reach for most sequences. Even so, neither settles whether there are infinitely many primes in the classical Lucas numbers, and neither makes the general set's infinitude any closer to proof. The strongest case for 'something happened' is therefore the broader reading, and even that case is partial.
what_would_settle_it: Settling the question itself needs a proof or disproof of infinitude, and nothing found suggests either exists. For this record's completeness, the following would close the gaps: the dated L(n) probable-prime and prime tables at primenumbers.net (Lifchitz PRP Top Records), which could not be reached; the OEIS A001606 revision history, to date the index additions after 2017; and the Prime Pages' full Lucas-number list below rank 20, to see proven primes smaller than 1770 digits. Reading the Ismailescu et al. (2025) and Broderius–Greene PDFs, and the body of arXiv 2609.08137, would confirm the statements that are currently from search summaries.
